Constellation

Constellation

Pulsar, Binary and Singularity: three playable pocket ribbon synths, modelled part by part from the public monotron, monotron DUO and monotron DELAY schematics and built on the Faust standard library. Nebula adds 43 space reverbs from Airwindows' open-source code, and Aurora 8 more from the Faust standard library and Mutable Instruments' Eurorack firmware.

Play either ribbon with a mouse or finger. The keys A to ] (A W S E D F T G Y H U J K O L P ; ' ]) play the instrument you touched last, marked "Keys"; the space bar toggles its Hold. "To Binary" and "To Singularity" patch an instrument into another's line in, so it plays through that one's filter (and Singularity's echo); the receiving instrument must be switched on. Chain Pulsar into Binary and Binary into Singularity to use all three, and any of them "To Nebula" or "To Aurora" for reverb; Nebula can feed Aurora too. A MIDI keyboard plays the same instrument once connected. Drag knobs up or down; double-click one to reset it. At full Peak a filter whistles on its own, without touching the ribbon.

Pulsar: where the numbers come from

Each stage follows the parts on the monotron schematic. Values tagged schematic are read or derived from it. hardware values come from the real unit's specification. Values tagged estimate need a real unit to calibrate.

StagePartsWhat the model doesSource
Ribbon spanQ1 IMX9, note at VR1"Whole ribbon Vbe offset 26.29 mV @ 20 °C" with Vt = 25.26 mV gives a 2.83× span: 18 semitones across the ribbon.schematic
VCO shapeC11, F2, IC3C/BFalling sawtooth (waveform icon at TP8), band-limited with os.sawtooth.schematic
GateIC2C, R51, C16, R52Touch detection drives the VCO/VCF gate: 0.1 ms attack (1k × 0.1 µF), 1 ms release (10k × 0.1 µF).schematic
LFO shapeC10, Q3, IC3E/DFalling ramp (icon at R64), restarted on every touch through the C9/R24 "LFO reset" pulse. The snap back up is band-limited with PolyBLEP.schematic
Filter key trackingR42 330k, R50 68k, R75The ribbon voltage also feeds the cutoff. Relative to the cutoff knob's 0–0.6 VCC span it adds 0.34 of the knob's range.schematic
Filter + resonanceQ12–14, C20, C21, IC4C, D1/D2Two-pole Korg 35 low-pass. The 1SS355 diodes in IC4C's feedback sit inside the resonance loop, so self-oscillation is soft-limited.schematic
Speaker pathC26, R80, R77, C27, R81, C30High-pass at 231 Hz and 72 Hz, low-pass at 5.9 kHz: the thin, bright sound of the built-in speaker.schematic
Headphone pathC25, R79, R82, C32High-pass at 2.3 Hz, otherwise flat.schematic
Pitch knob rangeVR3A, R18, R20, R211 V/octave over 0–10 V: 5 V centre, ±5 octaves. With 0 V = C0 assumed, the bottom of the ribbon runs from 16.4 Hz to 16.7 kHz, with C5 at the centre.hardware
LFO rate rangeVR4A, R28, Q4/Q6From 14 seconds per cycle (0.07 Hz) up to about 900 Hz, swept exponentially. The top of the range is well into audio rate. Below 1 Hz the knob shows seconds per cycle.hardware
LFO depthR4 2.2k, R44 10k, VR5AUp to 4 octaves of pitch, or most of the cutoff range.estimate

Binary: where the numbers come from

From the monotron DUO schematic. Its ribbon goes through an MSP430 microcontroller whose firmware isn't public, so the ribbon's range and scale snapping follow KORG's published feature list.

StagePartsWhat the model doesSource
Oscillators switchSW1A, R67 470k, R58 820kStandby, VCO1, or VCO1+2. VCO2 joins the mixer through 820k against VCO1's 470k, so it sits at 0.57 of VCO1's level.schematic
VCO shapeC13/C21, IC4, Q5–Q8Each core runs at twice the pitch and toggles a transistor flip-flop, giving 50% squares at SQR1 and SQR2. Band-limited with PolyBLEP.schematic
VCO2 pitchVR4A, R76, R62, R770–130 mV on Q3's base (VCC = 5 V, set by R4/R8): from unison up to +7.3 octaves above VCO1.schematic
X-ModR54, R59, VR3A, R55, R60SQR2 lifts VCO1's pitch while it is high: up to 3.1 octaves at full X-Mod Int. This is square-wave cross modulation.schematic
Filter trackingR70 (NU)The ribbon-to-cutoff resistor is marked not fitted, so on Binary the cutoff doesn't follow the ribbon.schematic
Filter, gate, ampQ11–13, D7/D8, Q10, IC6Same parts and values as the monotron, so both models share one filter, gate and amp.schematic
Scale buttonSW2A, IC2Cycles Chromatic, Major, Minor and Off. The bottom of the ribbon is the key note.hardware
Scale snappingIC2 firmwareSnaps to the nearest note of the scale (natural minor for Minor).estimate
Ribbon rangeIC2 firmwareTwo octaves across the ribbon.estimate
VCO1 pitch knobVR2A, R22Same 1 V/octave law as the monotron's Pitch knob.estimate

Singularity: where the numbers come from

From the monotron DELAY schematic. The echo is a PT2399 delay chip, so its timing comes from the chip's datasheet. datasheet values come from there.

StagePartsWhat the model doesSource
Echo routingVR7A, C20, R58 10k, IC4DThe echo never goes straight to the amp. It returns through the Feedback knob into the filter's input mixer, at 10× the VCO's gain (R58 10k vs R55 100k). So Feedback sets both echo level and repeats, and every repeat goes back through the filter.schematic
Delay timeIC5 PT2399, R80 1k, VR6A 100kElectric Druid's fit to the datasheet, ms = 11.46 × R(kΩ) + 29.7, gives 41 ms to 1.19 s. The time glides when you turn the knob, so echoes bend in pitch like tape.datasheet
Echo toneR74–R77, R82, C24, C25, C29, C31Two-pole filters at about 8.5 kHz either side of the chip.schematic
Echo darkeningPT2399 clockLonger delays run the chip's clock slower, so long echoes get darker: about 15 kHz at the shortest time, falling to 400 Hz at the longest.estimate
Feedback amountVR7ALoop gain 1.5 × Feedback: repeats build into runaway past about two-thirds of the knob. The filter's diodes keep it bounded.estimate
No filter gateQ10, R50 (NU)Not fitted, so the filter stays open between notes and echoes ring on after you let go.schematic
Fixed resonanceR78 3.3k, R73 5.6kNo Peak knob. Against the monotron's Peak pot plus R78 2.2k, this is 0.88 of full Peak's loop gain, where full Peak is the point of self-oscillation: strongly resonant, but it won't whistle on its own.schematic
Cutoff knobVR5A, R72 0 Ω, R48 68kThe knob spans 0–VCC instead of the monotron's 0–0.6 VCC into the same circuit, so it covers 1.67× more range. The filter is wide open from about 60% up. The ribbon adds 0.21 of the knob's span through R45 330k.schematic
LFOC9, F1, IC3D/E, SW1ATriangle or square, sent to pitch only, free-running.schematic
LFO shapeVR1 500k (rear trimmer)Skews the triangle or sets the square's width.hardware
Ribbon rangeR6 470k, R10 47k, R11, R15Four octaves, per KORG's spec. If the ribbon swung the full 5 V as on the monotron, these resistors would give about 11.6 octaves.hardware
Bottom of ribbonR22, R23, R24 (no pitch knob)55 Hz, so the ribbon runs from A1 to A5.estimate
LFO rate and depthVR3A, VR4A, R7 47k0.08–80 Hz, up to 3 octaves of pitch.estimate

Nebula: where the code comes from

Nebula runs all 42 reverbs in Airwindows' own Reverb category, plus StarChild2, all by Chris Johnson of Airwindows from his MIT-licensed source code. Each plugin's original C++ is compiled to WebAssembly unchanged, with a small stand-in for the VST plugin framework. A test builds the same C++ natively and compares: 81 of 86 test renders are bit-identical, and the rest match to 160 dB or better.

The selector's one-line descriptions are Chris Johnson's, from his Airwindopedia. Plugins that are fully wet by default start at 50% here, because an instrument patched in with "To Nebula" is heard only through Nebula. Knobs show each plugin's own readout where it has one (PocketVerbs' Type, kPlate's Damping); plain 0–1 controls show as percent. VerbSixes and VerbSevens are calibrated reference reverbs with no controls.

To keep knob moves from clicking, each change crossfades over 20 ms from the running reverb to an exact copy of it with the new setting.

Aurora: where the code comes from

Aurora gathers permissively licensed reverbs from three places. Nothing here is GPL.

ReverbSourceAuthorLicense
PlateFaust re.dattorro_revJakob Zerbian, after Jon Dattorro (1997)STK-4.3
ZitaFaust re.zita_rev1_stereoJulius O. Smith III, after Fons Adriaensen's zita-rev1STK-4.3
JPverb, GreyholeFaust re.jpverb, re.greyholeJulian Parker; Till BovermannMIT
FreeverbFaust re.stereo_freeverbRomain Michon, after JezarLGPL, with GRAME's exception for compiled code
Lyra, VirgoFaust re.valhallaSupermassive (copied into dsp/aurora/massive.lib)David BraunMIT
TextureRings reverb + stmlib (C++, unmodified)Emilie GilletMIT

The two "Deep space" reverbs, Lyra and Virgo, are David Braun's Faust models of two modes of Valhalla DSP's free ValhallaSupermassive, under the plug-in's mode names. Valhalla DSP did not make or endorse this project. Texture is the reverb from the Rings and Clouds Eurorack modules, renamed as the Mutable Instruments license asks of derivative works.

Texture is Rings' version, tuned for 48 kHz; at 44.1 kHz its delays run 9% longer. A native build of it matches the browser's bit for bit. Plate keeps Dattorro's delay lengths in samples at 29.8 kHz, so at 48 kHz it is a smaller plate.

Cloud Seed and four more Supermassive models (Gemini, Centaurus, Sagittarius, Great Annihilator) were here briefly. They were taken out because they cost the most to run (8–9% of a CPU core each) and to set up (up to 64 MB of delay lines each).

Aurora's knobs glide rather than jump. A sudden change inside a reverb's feedback loop (a gain, a diffusion coefficient, a delay length) clicks. So gains and coefficients ease in over about 20 ms, and delay times slew like a tape delay's time knob, bending the pitch by at most 25% while they move.

Every reverb in Nebula and Aurora is made, and run once silently, before sound starts. Making one while playing stalls the audio for 3–25 ms: Chrome compiles WebAssembly on first use, and allocating or freeing a large reverb's memory makes the browser stop for garbage collection. Both break up the sound. A reverb you switch away from rings out silently in the background, so switching back to it doesn't bring back an old tail. With nothing playing into it and its tail gone, Nebula or Aurora sleeps and costs nothing.

All the instruments and reverbs get their sines, exponentials and powers from musl's math library (MIT), compiled to WebAssembly along with them. Calling the browser's own Math.sin from WebAssembly creates a little garbage on every call. At several calls per sample, collecting it paused the audio often enough to crackle.
